div.p: Impact de l'ingestion aiguë de nitrate inorganique sur les performances réalisées lors d'un exercice de CrossFit ' Jackie ', chez des sportives entraînées : essai randomisé, contrôlé, contre placebo et en double aveugle

div.head: r é s u m é
div.p: Objectifs : Cette étude visait à évaluer les effets d'une supplémentation aiguë en nitrates sur la performance et quelques marqueurs de réponses physiologiques lors d'un exercice spécifique de CrossFit (Jackie) chez des athlètes féminines entraînées. Matériel et méthodes : Une étude croisée, randomisée, en double aveugle, contrôlée par placebo, a été menée auprès de 13 athlètes féminines de CrossFit (âge : 29,5 ± 7,5 ans, taille : 1,62 ± 0,04 m, masse corporelle : 68,7 ± 8,3 kg, pourcentage de masse grasse : 22,9 ± 4,5 %). Les participantes ont réalisé l'exercice Jackie (1000 m d'aviron, 50 thrusters (exercices d'enchaînement de squats et de développés militaires) et 30 tractions) 2,5 heures

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Nitric oxide (NO) is a central signaling molecule that regulates se veral physiological processes directly related to exercise performance, including vasodilation, skeletal muscle glucose uptake, contractility, mi tochondrial function, and angiogenesis [1,2]. While NO was initially believed to be produced exclusively via the oxidation of L-arginine me diated by nitric oxide synthase (NOS), evidence has demonstrated the existence of an alternative nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway, which becomes particularly relevant under hypoxic or acidic conditions where NOS ac tivity is limited [3,4]. This pathway has stimulated growing interest in dietary nitrate as an ergogenic aid, especially in exercise modalities characterized by high anaerobic demand [5].

Nitrate supplementation, commonly provided as beetroot juice, has been shown to increase circulating nitrate and nitrite concentra tions, thereby enhancing NO availability [6]. This improvement in NO bioavailability has been consistently associated with prolonged time to exhaustion and enhanced performance during high-intensity and short-duration exercise [7,8]. Proposed mechanisms include greater contractile efficiency, reduced energy cost, and improved muscle oxy gen utilization, with benefits observed across both short [9,10] and medium-duration protocols [11,12]. More recent studies indicate ad ditional effects, such as reduced muscle fatigue and improved recovery following intermittent exercise [13,14].

The physiological demands of CrossFit, a sport characterized by high-intensity, multi-modal efforts [15], align well with the proposed mechanisms of nitrate supplementation, such as improved contractile ef ficiency and muscle oxygen utilization [16]. This makes it a compelling model for investigating nitrate's ergogenic potential. However, findings in CrossFit athletes remain mixed. A chronic 6-day nitrate loading re gimen failed to enhance performance [17], whereas acute single-dose ingestion yielded benefits only when protocols incorporated structured 3-minute rest periods [18,19].

Despite the growing body of evidence supporting nitrate's ergoge nic potential, the research is overwhelmingly skewed towards male participants, a significant bias that limits the applicability of current findings to female athletes [20][21][22]. Direct extrapolation of results is tenuous, as women exhibit distinct physiological differences that can fundamentally alter the response to nitrate supplementation. For ins tance, fluctuations in estrogen across the menstrual cycle are known to influence endogenous nitric oxide (NO) production via upregulation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), which can lead to higher ba seline plasma nitrite concentrations and potentially blunt the ergogenic effect of exogenous nitrate [23]. Furthermore, potential sex-specific dif ferences in muscle fiber typology and substrate metabolism could also modulate performance outcomes [24,25]. The sparse literature that has included female cohorts reflects this complexity, presenting equivocal results that have failed to establish a clear consensus [21,23,26,27]. This notable gap underscores the critical need for well-controlled studies specifically designed to investigate the efficacy of nitrate sup plementation in trained female athletes, thereby justifying the present research.

CrossFit 's popularity among women and its reliance on repeated high-intensity efforts make it a relevant model for investigating the er gogenic potential of nitrate. This potential is particularly promising for CrossFit , as a meta-analysis by Silva et al. [21] found nitrate sup plementation to be most effective in exercises lasting 2-10 minutes, a duration that aligns with benchmark workouts like Jackie. Therefore, we hypothesized that acute ingestion of nitrate-rich beetroot juice two and a half hours before exercise would enhance performance in this spe cific context. The aim of the present study was to test this hypothesis by investigating the acute effects of dietary nitrate on performance during the "Jackie" workout in trained female athletes.

div.head: Ethical approval
div.p: This study was designed as a randomized, double-blind, placebocontrolled crossover trial. The research protocol was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of the Federal University of Lavras under approval number 5.966.790. All participants provided written informed consent prior to study commencement, following a detailed ex planation of the experimental procedures, associated risks, and benefits of participation.

div.head: Experimental design
div.p: Data collection was conducted over four sessions. During the first visit, participants were provided with detailed information about the study's objectives and experimental procedures, after which they read and signed an informed consent form. This was followed by anthropo metric assessment and familiarization with the benchmark Jackie. Prior to the performance test, participants completed a standardized 5-minute warm-up. During the second visit, participants completed a second fa miliarization trial with the Jackie workout. Following the collection of baseline data (blood lactate, resting blood pressure, and heart rate), the workout was performed. Immediately upon completion, post-exercise blood lactate and ratings of perceived exertion (RPE) were recorded. The peak heart rate achieved during the Jackie workout was also noted.

For the third and fourth visits, participants were randomized to ingest either nitrate-rich beetroot juice or nitrate-depleted placebo 2.5 hours before the performance test. Participants (n = 15) were ran domly assigned to one of two intervention sequences (Treatment A then B; or Treatment B then A) using a computer-generated list from rando mizer.org. The randomization sequence was generated and stored by an independent researcher who had no involvement in data collection. This researcher prepared and labelled all supplementation bottles with non-identifiable alphanumeric codes corresponding to each condition, thereby ensuring full allocation concealment. Both participants and in vestigators remained blinded to treatment assignment throughout all testing sessions. This process ensured maximal counterbalancing, with eight participants starting with Treatment A and seven with Treat ment B. To maintain double-blinding, treatments were pre-coded by an independent researcher, and both participants and experimenters remai ned unaware of the specific treatment administered in each session. As most participants included in this study (84.6%) indicated via a Google Forms questionnaire a perceived decline in performance during the premenstrual and menstrual phases, all testing sessions were scheduled to begin on the fourth day after the menstrual period to mitigate the in fluence of this variable. All sessions were completed within a 10-to 14-day window.

div.head: Participants
div.p: Initially, a convenience sample comprising fifteen women was recruited for the study based on a preliminary online screening ques tionnaire (Google Forms). Key inclusion criteria for enrolment included: age between 18-40 years, a minimum of one year of CrossFit trai ning experience, a "regular" menstrual cycle (defined as a cycle duration between 21 and 35 days with regular menses). Exclusion criteria com prised: the presence of chronic diseases, musculoskeletal limitations, recent use (within the past three months) of performance supplements (e.g., creatine, beta-alanine), and any history of anabolic steroid use. All fifteen enrolled participants underwent randomization and completed the preliminary familiarization session; however, two participants with drew for personal reasons prior to the first experimental testing session. Therefore, thirteen female CrossFit practitioners successfully comple ted all study procedures and were included in the final analysis. Their mean (± SD) characteristics were: age, 29.5 ± 7.5 years; body mass, 68.7 ± 8.3 kg; stature, 1.62 ± 0.04 m; body fat, 22.9 ± 4.5%. Participants had an average of 3.5 ± 2.4 years of CrossFit training experience, with a training frequency of 4.6 ± 0.9 sessions per week.

div.head: Familiarization and baseline assessments
div.p: During the first session, after providing informed consent, partici pants underwent anthropometric evaluation (body mass, height, and body fat percentage). Body density was determined using the seven-site skinfold protocol by Jackson and Pollock [28], and body fat percentage was estimated using the Siri equation [29]. During this visit, participants were also familiarized with the Jackie workout.

To standardize dietary intake, a 24-hour dietary recall was conduc ted by a nutritionist during the second visit. Participants were instructed to maintain their habitual diet throughout the study and to replicate their food intake from the day preceding visit 2 on all subsequent ex perimental visits (visits 3 and 4). The 24-hour dietary recall from visit 2 was sent to participants via WhatsApp two days prior to each expe rimental visit to serve as a personalized guide for each participant to facilitate this dietary standardization. On each experimental day, ver bal confirmation was obtained from participants to ensure adherence to their prescribed dietary intake. Participants were instructed to avoid nitrate-rich foods and alcoholic beverages for 24 hours prior to each ex perimental test. To support adherence to these dietary restrictions, a detailed list of foods rich in nitrate was provided to each participant. Visit 2 also served as a second familiarization session for the Jackie wor kout. During this visit, participants performed the workout to reinforce technique and pacing. Furthermore, familiarization with the physiologi cal measurements (resting blood pressure, heart rate, and blood lactate) and Ratings of Perceived Exertion (RPE) was conducted.

div.head: Supplementation protocol
div.p: The supplementation was administered two hours prior to arrival at the laboratory, which corresponded to 2.5 hours before the com mencement of the performance test. In a randomized, double-blind manner, participants ingested 70 mL of either concentrated beetroot juice (containing approximately 6.4 mmol [400 mg] of nitrate) or an isovolumetric, nitrate-depleted placebo (∼0.0055 mmol of NO 3 -) (Beet IT; James White Drinks Ltd., Ipswich, UK). A washout period of at least four days was implemented between the third and fourth visits. Additio nally, they were advised to refrain from using antibacterial mouthwash, brushing or scraping their tongue, and chewing gum during this per iod to preserve the oral microbiota essential for the reduction of nitrate to nitrite, a critical step for nitric oxide production and its subsequent ergogenic effects [21].

div.head: Performance test (Jackie)
div.p: Performance tests were conducted at the NanBox affiliate, located in the [city name], State of [state name], at the same time of day for each participant to control for circadian effects. Participants were ins tructed to maintain a regular sleep pattern, and refrain from intense exercise in the 48 hours preceding each test. Upon arrival, participants rested in a seated position for 10 minutes. Baseline measurements of blood pressure, blood lactate, and resting heart rate were then taken.

Participants then performed a standardized warm-up consisting of a 200-m row on a Concept2 rower (Model M3, Damper setting 5), follo wed by a circuit of three exercises performed in sequence: 10 push-ups, 10 ring rows (with the body inclined at approximately 45 ∘ ), and 10 un loaded squats. The circuit was repeated three times. This warm-up was designed to gradually elevate heart rate, promote neuromuscular activa tion, and provide a physiological preparation specific to the upcoming task. After a 2-minute rest, participants began the "Jackie" workout for time, which consists of: a 1000-meter row, 50 thrusters (with a 15 kg barbell), and 30 pull-ups (Fig. 1). Participants were instructed to com plete the workout as fast as possible. No verbal encouragement was provided during the test.

div.head: Rowing
div.p: The 1000-meter row was performed on a calibrated Concept2 ro wer. Participants were seated and executed the movement through leg extension and arm flexion, pulling the handle to the abdomen before re turning to the start position. Thruster: The thruster exercise began with the barbell in a "front rack" position. Participants squatted to a depth below parallel (hip crease below the knee) and then performed a conti nuous movement, extending the hips and knees and finishing with a press to lock out the arms overhead.

div.head: Pull-up
div.p: The 30 pull-ups were performed using the "kipping" style, where participants initiated the movement from a full hang, used a hip swing to generate momentum, and pulled until their chin cleared the bar before returning to the full hang position.

All thruster and pull-up repetitions were judged for validity by a CrossFit -certified judge. Equipment was calibrated before each ses sion, and the same barbell and weight were used for all participants. Pull-up bar height was adjusted to each participant's preference. Imme diately following the test, RPE, peak heart rate, and blood lactate were recorded.

div.head: Blood lactate
div.p: Capillary blood samples were collected from the participant's fin gertip at two time points: at rest (pre-warm-up) and immediately post-"Jackie" workout. The initial drop of blood was discarded. Ap proximately 1-2 μL of fresh blood was then applied to a lactate-specific test strip (Accusport BM -Lactate, Roche , Hawthorne, USA) and analyzed using a portable lactate analyzer (Accusport, Boehringer Mannheim -Roche , Hawthorne, USA). Delta blood lactate (Δ[La]) was calculated as the difference between post-workout and pre-warm-up resting values (Δ[La] = [La] post -[La] rest ).

div.head: Ratings of perceived exertion (RPE)
div.p: Immediately upon completion of the Jackie workout, RPE was deter mined using the Borg CR-10 scale. Participants were instructed to report their overall level of exertion for the entire exercise session, based on a scale ranging from 0 (representing no exertion at all) to 10 (representing maximal exertion) [30].

div.head: Blood pressure (BP) and heart rate (HR)
div.p: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure was measured at rest prior to the warm-up using an automated monitor (Omron , Kyoto, Japan). Mea surements were taken with participants seated, feet flat on the floor, and back supported, following the guidelines of the Brazilian Society of Cardiology [31]. Heart rate was recorded continuously throughout the protocol with a commercial monitor (Forerunner 310XT, Garmin, USA). Resting heart rate (HR rest ) was measured in a seated position fol lowing a 10-minute quiet rest prior to the warm-up. The highest heart rate value achieved during the "Jackie" performance test was designated as the peak heart rate (HRpeak). Delta heart rate (ΔHR) was calcu lated as the difference between peak heart rate and resting heart rate (ΔHR = HR peak -HR rest ).

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: Data were analyzed using linear mixed models (LMM) to evaluate the effects of Treatment (Nitrate vs. Placebo). To minimize intra-subject va riance, values from the familiarization session were included as a fixed covariate. Treatment and moment (Test 1 vs. Test 2) were defined as fixed effects to account for potential order effects, while subject iden tification was included as a random intercept for the crossover design. Post-hoc comparisons were performed using estimated marginal means (EMMs). Effect sizes (Hedges' g) were calculated by dividing the mean difference by the pooled residual standard deviation, applying a correc tion factor for the sample size. Analyses were conducted in SPSS (v.26.0, IBM Corp.), with significance set at P ≤ 0.05.

div.head: Overall outcomes
div.p: The LMM revealed no significant main effects for treatment or moment across all variables (all P > 0.05). The inclusion of the fami liarization session as a covariate adjusted for baseline variance did not reveal significant differences between conditions. Effect sizes for all comparisons were trivial to small (Table 1).

div.head: Performance outcomes
div.p: There was no difference in Jackie performance between the ni trate and placebo conditions (Nitrate: 553.7 ± 18.6 s vs. Placebo: 561.0 ± 18.6 s; P = 0.468; g = 0.27) (Fig. 2).

div.head: Hemodynamic and physiological responses
div.p: No significant differences were observed between Nitrate and Pla cebo for systolic blood pressure (117.8 ± 2.6 vs. 119.0 ± 2.6 mmHg; P = 0.731; g = 0.13) or diastolic blood pressure (71.3 ± 2.8 vs. 71.8 ± 2.8 mmHg; P = 0.839; g = 0.04). Similarly, ΔHR did not differ between conditions (Nitrate: 107.4 ± 2.0 vs. Placebo: 107.9 ± 2.0 bpm; P = 0.772; g = 0.11).

div.head: Metabolic and perceptual outcomes
div.p: Blood lactate accumulation (Δ[La]) was unaffected by supplemen tation (Nitrate: 11.5 ± 0.6 vs. Placebo: 12.4 ± 0.6 mmol/L; P = 0.296; g = 0.36). Rating of perceived exertion (RPE) was similar bet ween conditions (Nitrate: 7.5 ± 0.3 vs. Placebo: 7.4 ± 0.3; P = 0.651; g = 0.12).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: The primary purpose of the present study was to investigate the acute effects of nitrate supplementation, delivered via beetroot juice (6.4 mmol), on the performance of trained female CrossFit athletes during the benchmark Jackie. To our knowledge, this is the first in vestigation to examine the ergogenic potential of nitrate in this specific, underrepresented demographic using a standardized and widely reco gnized CrossFit test. The principal finding of this study was that a single dose of nitrate provided no ergogenic benefit during the Cross fit Jackie in females. Congruently, supplementation failed to elicit any significant changes in secondary physiological or perceptual measures, including blood lactate concentration, resting or peak heart rate, resting blood pressure, or RPE. This finding addresses a critical gap and chal lenging the broad applicability of nitrate as a universal performance enhancer, particularly within female athletic populations engaged in high-intensity functional training.

Our findings contribute to the evolving understanding of nitrate supplementation, particularly in female populations, where existing li terature remains predominantly focused on male participants [20,21]. While physiological differences often prevent direct extrapolation of male-centric findings to female athletes, our results, demonstrating no nitrate performance benefit for the Jackie workout in women, suggest either a sex-specific blunted response or simply that nitrate supplemen tation may not be a potent ergogenic aid for this specific high-intensity intermittent task, regardless of sex. This highlights the need for further research directly investigating nitrate efficacy in both sexes for diverse performance modalities.

The apparent sexual dimorphism in the nitrate response is likely mul tifactorial, rooted in physiological distinctions such as the influence of estrogen, differences in muscle fiber composition, and potential varia tions in oral microbiota [25,32,33]. This complexity supports emerging evidence suggesting a potentially lower efficacy of nitrate supplementa tion in women. Investigations across various performance modalities, including endurance exercise, high-intensity running, and repeated sprint protocols in active women, have generally failed to demonstrate performance improvements following either acute or chronic nitrate supplementation [23,25,27,34]. Our study extends these consistent null findings to the specific, high-intensity functional movements characte ristic of a CrossFit WOD. Despite this, the modest number of studies conducted exclusively in female cohorts, coupled with their methodo logical heterogeneity (including varying exercise types, doses, timing of ingestion, practices for controlling oral microbiota, and the absence of menstrual cycle phase control), suggests caution is warranted be fore definitively concluding that nitrate does not benefit performance in women [22].

A comprehensive meta-analysis by Silva et al. [21] concluded that nitrate's ergogenic effects are most reliably observed during severeintensity exercise lasting between 2 and 10 minutes. The Jackie WOD, selected for performance evaluation in the present study, aligns with these characteristics: it was performed at a high intensity, as demons trated by the expressive increase in blood lactate during the WOD, and had an average duration below 10 minutes. The fact that the athletes did not improve performance, despite these optimal charac teristics, suggests that other factors, such as the nature of the effort or inherent sex-specific differences, may have influenced the observed results.

The Jackie WOD demands a singular, all-out effort with no pro grammed rest until completion. In the present study, participants were instructed to complete the exercises as rapidly as possible. During highintensity effort like Jackie, the primary driver of fatigue is the rapid accumulation of metabolic by products, leading to severe metabolic acidosis. While this low-pH environment theoretically facilitates the non-enzymatic reduction of nitrite to bioactive NO [4], acute nitrate supplementation nonetheless failed to promote performance improve ment in our participants. This suggests that the metabolic stress and resulting fatigue may have been too profound for the subtle ergogenic benefits of NO to be fully expressed.

Garnacho-Castaño et al. [18] investigated nitrate supplementation in male CrossFit athletes using an intermittent protocol of two sets of 90s of wall balls plus 60s of full back squats. Crucially, a 3-minute passive rest period was included between the exercises only during the first set, where nitrate significantly increased the number of comple ted repetitions. No performance benefit was observed in the second set, which lacked programmed rest period, similar to the continuous nature of our "Jackie" protocol. A similar lack of ergogenic effect was observed by Kramer et al. [17] during the "Grace" workout (30 clean-and-jerks completed as fast as possible without rest). However, unlike the acute single-dose regimens evaluated in our study and other [18], Kramer et al. utilized a chronic 6-day nitrate-loading protocol. Taken together, these comparative results suggest that the absence of structured reco very periods may limit nitrate's ergogenic potential across both acute and chronic supplementation strategies. However, further research is necessary to confirm this hypothesis and determine the optimal rest du ration and exercise structure required to elicit a beneficial effect of the nitrate supplementation.

The absence of significant alterations in our secondary physiological measures further corroborates our primary finding. The lack of effect on resting blood pressure and heart rate is consistent with a large body of literature demonstrating that trained, normotensive individuals, and particularly women who tend to have lower baseline blood pressure, do not demonstrate measurable cardiovascular responses to nitrate sup plementation [4,25,35,36]. Furthermore, the timing of our assessment (2 hours post-ingestion) and the moderate dose (6.4 mmol) may have been suboptimal, as peak hypotensive effects have typically been noted at later time points (∼4 hours) and with higher doses (> 8.4 mmol) in some male cohorts [6].

This study has limitations that warrant acknowledgment. While our sample size is comparable to previous investigations within the CrossFit domain [17,18], an a priori sample size calculation was not performed, and a convenience sample was used. Consequently, it is pos sible that the study was underpowered to detect very small or subtle effects of nitrate. Our findings should be interpreted with these consi derations in mind, following current recommendations for sample size justification [37]. A crucial limitation was the absence of plasma ni trate and nitrite measurements. This prevents direct confirmation that participants achieved adequate plasma concentrations, though this was mitigated by standardizing ingestion two hours pre-exercise, a time frame robustly associated with peak bioavailability [21]. Additionally, baseline capillary blood lactate was sampled at rest prior to the standar dized warm-up rather than immediately before initiating the "Jackie" workout. Consequently, the reported Δ[La] reflects the cumulative lac tate accumulation from both the warm-up protocol and the primary experimental workout. Finally, while we pragmatically controlled for the menstrual cycle by scheduling tests based on participant self-reports to avoid phases of perceived performance decrement, this perception was not corroborated by any physiological evaluation, and the mens trual cycle phases were not biochemically confirmed. We contend, however, that excluding women from research for this reason is unjusti fiable, especially as recent evidence suggests the menstrual cycle phase may not interact with nitrate's ergogenic effects [23,38].

Despite these limitations, this study offers significant and timely contributions to a relatively unexplored area of sports nutrition. Female athletes remain markedly underrepresented in nitrate supplementa tion research, and CrossFit , a rapidly growing sport among women, has received limited scientific attention. Importantly, this investigation incorporated several methodological strengths that enhance the robust ness and applicability of its findings, including the use of a randomized, double-blind, crossover design, menstrual-cycle-informed scheduling, and the application of a placebo beverage matched to the nitrate-rich supplement in flavor profile and presentation. This approach streng thens blinding procedures and supports the internal validity of the study. Furthermore, by employing a standardized and widely recogni zed benchmark workout, the study provides ecologically meaningful, sex-specific evidence that can directly inform nutritionists, practitio ners and researchers. These results refine expectations regarding nitrate supplementation in women and underscore the need for sex-specific re search on ergogenic aids, emphasizing the broader scientific relevance and practical impact of this work.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Acute nitrate supplementation did not enhance performance in female CrossFit athletes completing the Benchmark 'Jackie' WOD. Furthermore, nitrate did not modify any of the measured physiologi cal responses or RPE. However, this study provides the first controlled evidence evaluating the acute effects of nitrate supplementation in trained women, addressing a notable gap in a literature predomi nantly based on male samples. Although no ergogenic effects were observed, the present findings offer an initial reference point for contex tualizing the expected impact of acute nitrate use in trained female athletes and underscore the need for further sex-specific investiga tions before translating nitrate supplementation strategies into practical application.
